Setting up a grading pipeline

Source: vignettes/grading-pipeline.Rmd
grading-pipeline.Rmd

Versión en español

This vignette walks through a complete grading run end to end: writing tests, gathering submissions, grading, summarising, and exporting.

Folder layout

The grader expects one sub-folder per student under a submissions root, and a flat folder of test files. File names follow a simple convention:

submissions/
  garcia_juan/
    ejercicio1.R
    ejercicio2.R
  lopez_maria/
    ejercicio1.R
    ejercicio2.R

tests/
  test_ejercicio1.R
  test_ejercicio2.R

A test file holds one or more functions named test_<exercise>_<case> that return TRUE or FALSE.

# tests/test_ejercicio1.R
test_ejercicio1_roots <- function() {
  all(quadratic_roots(1, 0, -1) == c(-1, 1))
}
test_ejercicio1_numeric <- function() {
  is.numeric(quadratic_roots(1, 0, -1))
}

Running the grader 

library(corrector)

results <- grade_submissions("submissions/", test_dir = "tests/")

results is a grade_results object: a long-format data frame with one row per test, plus the columns student, exercise, status, message, and duration. Status is one of pass, fail, error, timeout, missing, or source_error.

head(as.data.frame(results, format = "long"))

Convert to the legacy wide-boolean view with as.data.frame(results, format = "wide").

Summarising

grade_report() reduces the long results to per-exercise pass rates and per-student scores, plus counts of errors, timeouts, and missing submissions.

grade_report(results)

plot_report() produces three plots. Pass backend = "ggplot2" to use ggplot2, if installed.

Exporting 

export_to_csv(results, "grades.csv")               # wide by default
export_to_csv(results, "grades-long.csv", format = "long")
export_to_html(results, "report.html")

The HTML report colour-codes each cell by status and includes a per-student breakdown of every test.

Partial credit, weights and feedback

student_scores() gives each exercise the fraction of its tests that pass, with optional weights per test or per exercise, and a total grade where a missing exercise counts as 0. grade_report(scoring = "partial") uses the same rules. grade_scale() turns that score into a grade (1 to 10 with 60% as a 4, by default). export_feedback() writes one Markdown file per student, in Spanish or English depending on lang.

grades <- student_scores(results, weights = c(ejercicio2 = 2))
grades$grade <- grade_scale(grades$total)
export_feedback(results, "feedback/", lang = "en")

Similar submissions

compare_submissions() lists, for each exercise, the pairs of students with very similar files, even after renaming variables or changing spacing or comments. A high similarity does not prove copying; use it to pick what to read by hand.

compare_submissions("submissions/", min_similarity = 0.8)

testthat, R Markdown and Quarto

Test functions can use testthat expectations (library(testthat) at the top of the test file). Students can hand in .R, .Rmd or .qmd files, and file names are matched ignoring case.

Timeouts and untrusted code

The default engine, "callr", runs each exercise in a fresh R subprocess with a temporary working directory. Each test gets timeout seconds (default 10), and so does loading the student’s file. If a test does not respond to the limit (for example inside Sys.sleep()), the subprocess is killed once the whole exercise passes timeout × number of tests + 5 seconds; tests that already finished keep their result. Use timeout = Inf for no limit.

results <- grade_submissions("submissions/", test_dir = "tests/", timeout = 30)

engine = "inproc" runs tests in the current R session. It is faster, but setTimeLimit() does not interrupt every loop, and student code can change your global environment.

For large classes, workers runs several subprocesses at the same time:

results <- grade_submissions("submissions/", test_dir = "tests/", workers = 4)

corrector is not a sandbox. The callr engine protects your R session, not your computer: student code can read and write any file your user can, use the network, or run system commands. For code from people you do not trust, run corrector inside a container or virtual machine without your credentials. The callr and inproc engines block the common cheating tricks and report the rest; engine = "isolated" keeps student code out of the process that runs the tests. See vignette("cheat-resistant-grading").

Renaming students

The default student-name extractor takes the first underscore-separated segment and applies title case (so garcia_juan_12345 becomes Garcia). Pass student_name_fn to override:

results <- grade_submissions(
  "submissions/", test_dir = "tests/",
  student_name_fn = function(folder) {
    sub("_.*$", "", folder)
  }
)

Moodle

layout = "moodle" reads the .zip from Moodle’s “Download all submissions”, with or without “Download submissions in folders”:

results <- grade_submissions("assignment1.zip", test_dir = "tests/",
                             layout = "moodle")

To send the grades back, export_moodle_feedback() builds a .zip with one feedback file inside each student’s Moodle folder. On the assignment’s submissions page, use “Upload multiple feedback files in a zip”; the assignment must have file feedback turned on.

export_moodle_feedback(results, "feedback-assignment1.zip")
